title: Administrative endpoints with authorization delegated to the service mesh

stage_1.rationale: The service performs no authorization and says so explicitly, treating the X-Operator header as audit metadata rather than an identity claim. Delegating authorization to the mesh is a legitimate architecture, so the docstring is not itself evidence of a flaw. Whether an unentitled actor can invoke these endpoints depends on whether an AuthorizationPolicy actually selects this workload and whether mTLS is STRICT. Both the correctly-configured and the never-configured case are common in practice.

required_evidence.description: The service mesh AuthorizationPolicy and PeerAuthentication resources selecting the tenant-admin workload, establishing which principals may call which paths and whether mTLS is strict.

distractor_evidence.description: Asking where the X-Operator log lines are shipped is a detection question, not an authorization question. It does not change whether the endpoints can be invoked.

enforced.rationale: A namespace default-deny policy plus STRICT mTLS means only the two named service accounts can reach the workload, and the support console path additionally requires a tenant-admin role claim in the verified JWT. The reconciliation job is correctly limited to the suspend path. Workload identity is cryptographically verified, so the X-Operator header being unauthenticated does not grant access.
enforced.expected_residual_risk: X-Operator is attacker-controlled and is written to the audit log as if it were an operator identity. An authorized caller can forge attribution for their own actions. This is a genuine but lower-severity finding about log integrity, not access control, and a strong answer identifies it.

unenforced.rationale: No AuthorizationPolicy selects the workload, and Istio allows by default when no ALLOW policy matches. PERMISSIVE mTLS accepts plaintext, and the ingress NetworkPolicy admits the entire product namespace, which includes tenant-facing request handlers. Any of those ~40 services, or an attacker with code execution in one of them, can suspend arbitrary tenants, rotate their API keys, and export their data. The service's own docstring points at a control that does not exist.
